adc-dac-030.summary: JA explanation says Nyquist-rate ADCs sample at 'about twice the Nyquist frequency'. dram-002.summary: '規格では通常64 ms以内に全行を一巡' is presented as the general rule; DDR5 and LPDDR4/5 use a 32 ms refresh window in the normal temperature range.
dram-002.basis: DDR5 tREFI = 3.9 us (normal mode) x 8192 REF commands = 32 ms; DDR4 7.8 us x 8192 = 64 ms.
dram-002.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

dram-007.summary: Says one row activation reads 'several KB' into the sense amplifiers. Per DRAM chip the page (row) size is 1-2 KB (DDR4/DDR5 x4/x8: 1 KB, x16: 2 KB); 'several KB' (~8 KB) only applies to a whole 64-bit rank. It is also inconsistent with the preceding 'thousands of cells per word line' (thousands of bits ~ 1 KB).
dram-007.basis: JEDEC DDR4/DDR5 page sizes: 1 KB (x4, x8), 2 KB (x16). 8192 bits = 1 KB.
dram-007.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

dram-036.summary: States that DDR-family DRAMs refresh all rows within 64 ms; true for DDR3/DDR4, but DDR5 (tREFI 3.9 us x 8192 REF) and LPDDR4/5 use a ~32 ms window in the normal temperature range. Answer (64 ms is closest) is unaffected.
dram-036.basis: Micron DDR5 new-features white paper: all-bank REF issued on average every 3.9 us in normal mode (vs 7.8 us in DDR4); 8192 x 3.9 us = 32 ms. LPDDR4/5 tREFW = 32 ms. The explanation presents 64 ms as the rule for all DDR generations.
dram-036.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

dram-038.summary: JA choice and explanation say burst data is transferred 'クロックごとに' (once per clock), but DDR transfers on both clock edges (BL8 takes 4 clocks); this contradicts dram-006. EN explanation already says 'one per clock edge', so JA and EN also differ.
dram-038.basis: DDR4 BL8 occupies 4 tCK on the data bus (2 transfers per clock).
dram-038.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

dram-047.summary: Implies the prefetch doubled every generation up to DDR4 (DDR 2n, DDR2 4n, ... DDR4 8n). DDR3 already used 8n prefetch; DDR4 kept 8n and raised speed with bank groups instead, so the 'doubled each generation' claim is wrong for DDR3->DDR4.
dram-047.basis: JEDEC DDR3 (JESD79-3) and DDR4 (JESD79-4) both specify 8n prefetch / BL8; DDR4 introduced bank groups to reach higher data rates without a 16n prefetch. DDR5 moved to 16n.
dram-047.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

eda-032.basis: JA: 「ドイツのSiemensのEDA部門(旧Mentor Graphics)」 = the EDA division of Germany's Siemens. Mentor Graphics/Siemens EDA has been based in Wilsonville, Oregon since before the 2017 acquisition.

ehs-042.summary: EN says PRTR is 'under the Chemical Substances Control Law'. The JA says 化管法 (the PRTR Law, Act on Confirmation of Release Amounts of Specific Chemical Substances in the Environment and Promotion of Improvements to the Management Thereof). 'Chemical Substances Control Law' is the usual English name of a different law, 化審法 (CSCL), so the EN text names the wrong law.
ehs-042.basis: Japan's PRTR system comes from the 1999 化学物質排出把握管理促進法 (化管法, often called the PRTR Law). The Chemical Substances Control Law (化審法, 1973) covers the evaluation and regulation of manufacturing and importing new chemicals, and it has no PRTR reporting.

emerging-memory-009.summary: Gives the reset pulse width as 'tens to hundreds of ns', the same range emerging-memory-039 gives for set while saying set is slower than reset. Reset pulses are typically short (~10-50 ns); hundreds of ns is the set regime.
emerging-memory-009.basis: Standard PCM operation: short high-amplitude reset pulse (~tens of ns or less) vs longer lower-amplitude set pulse (~100 ns or more); the item's own sibling (039) states set is the slower operation.

emerging-memory-020.summary: JA explanation says the resistance rises 'proportional to the logarithm of time' but then gives the power law R ∝ t^ν; these contradict (power law means log R is linear in log t). The EN text correctly says 'as a power of time', so JA and EN also disagree.

etching-032.summary: States etch-tool plasmas have an ionization fraction of about 0.01% or less. That holds for typical CCP, but high-density ICP plasmas (10^11-10^12 cm^-3 at ~1 Pa, as stated in etching-015) are ~0.04-0.4% ionized, so the figure is too low as a general statement and conflicts with etching-015.

finfet-030.summary: 'CFETもこの一種です' presents CFET as unconditionally a form of sequential monolithic 3D. The main CFET approach (monolithic CFET) builds both n and p devices from one Si/SiGe stack in one flow and does not build a second tier on top. Only sequential CFET fits the definition given in the explanation.
finfet-030.basis: CFET has two integration schemes: monolithic CFET (one stacked-nanosheet epi, both devices formed together, the approach shown by imec, Intel and TSMC) and sequential CFET (top layer bonded and processed after the bottom device). The explanation defines monolithic 3D as forming the 2nd transistor layer after the 1st is done, which applies only to the sequential variant.
finfet-030.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

finfet-049.summary: Overstates the quantum-confinement Vth sensitivity: at ~5 nm body thickness a one-monolayer (0.3 nm) change shifts the lowest subband by only a few meV (well below 'tens of mV'); tens of mV per monolayer occurs only at ~2-3 nm and below.
finfet-049.basis: Infinite-well estimate dE = hbar^2 pi^2 / (2 m* t^2) (an upper bound; finite barriers give less). For a (100) sheet the lowest subband uses m*=0.916 m0: E(5 nm)=16.4 meV, E(4.7 nm)-E(5 nm)=2.2 meV. With m*=0.315 (Δ4 valleys, (110) fin sidewall) it is about 6 meV, and even the light mass 0.19 gives about 10 meV. Tens of mV per monolayer appears at t≈2-3 nm (m*=0.916, t=2 nm: about 39 meV). This matches the ultrathin-body SOI experiments in which the Vth shift rises steeply only below about 4 nm.
finfet-049.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

gpu-programming-014.summary: Claims the strided a[i*32] access moves "tens of times" more data than a[i]. On current NVIDIA GPUs global memory is transferred in 32-byte sectors, so each thread pulls one 32-byte sector: 32x32 B = 1024 B vs 128 B, i.e. 8x. The 32x figure only holds for 128-byte transaction granularity.
gpu-programming-014.basis: a[i]: 32 threads x 4 B = 128 B = 4 sectors. a[i*32]: 32 distinct 128-B-apart addresses -> 32 sectors x 32 B = 1024 B (8x); with 128-B lines 4096 B (32x). Since Maxwell/Pascal, L2/DRAM access granularity is 32-B sectors (CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide, coalesced access section).
gpu-programming-014.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

hdl-verification-027.summary: The explanation's fix is wrong for this code: it says declaring the signals 'wire signed [7:0]' makes the comparison give 0, but the other operand is 8'd1, a sized literal that is unsigned, so the expression stays unsigned and gt remains 1. It also refers to 'a and b' although the code has no b. The EN explanation repeats the wrong fix.
hdl-verification-027.basis: IEEE 1364-2005 / 1800: sized or based constants (e.g. 8'd1) are unsigned unless the 's' designator is used (8'sd1). If any operand of a relational expression is unsigned, the whole expression is evaluated as unsigned. So with 'wire signed [7:0] a = 8'hFF;', 'a > 8'd1' still compares 255 > 1 and gives 1; 'a > 8'sd1' (or the unsized signed literal 1) gives -1 > 1 = 0. The explanation itself states the 'one unsigned operand makes it all unsigned' rule, which contradicts its own fix.
hdl-verification-027.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

hw-security-031.summary: The explanation says, without qualification, that processing a chip to read a PUF value changes the variation itself. That is a design goal of some PUFs, such as coating PUFs or PUFs with a tamper-sensitive layer, but not a general property. Researchers have read out and even cloned SRAM PUF start-up values by semi-invasive methods (photonic emission analysis plus FIB edits). (EN: same claim.)
hw-security-031.basis: Helfmeier, Boit, Nedospasov, Seifert, 'Cloning Physically Unclonable Functions' (HOST 2013) read out an SRAM PUF's start-up pattern through the chip backside and cloned it with FIB, so reading did not destroy the variation. Tamper-evidence holds only for some PUF types.
hw-security-031.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

image-sensor-039.summary: Calls the CCD blooming streak 'smear'. Smear is a distinct CCD artifact (light/charge leaking into the vertical transfer register during readout) that occurs even without pixel saturation; blooming in CCDs spreads along the column, but it is not called smear.
image-sensor-039.basis: Standard CCD terminology distinguishes blooming (overflow of saturated wells, mainly along the column) from smear (vertical streak from light reaching the VCCD during transfer). Conflating them may mislead learners.
image-sensor-039.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

image-sensor-041.summary: Note for choice 0 claims visible light is not used to measure object temperature at all; optical/radiation pyrometers measure hot objects (roughly >700 °C) using visible/near-IR light. It is only true for room-temperature thermography.
image-sensor-041.basis: By Wien's law, very hot objects radiate significantly in the visible/NIR, and disappearing-filament and ratio pyrometers use those bands. The point is that room-temperature objects emit essentially no visible light.
image-sensor-041.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

image-sensor-048.summary: PTC relation is written as variance = mean × (1/K) while K is defined as output per electron (DN/e-). With K in DN/e-, variance(DN²) = K × mean(DN); the stated formula would give 1/K from the slope, contradicting the definition.
image-sensor-048.basis: S_DN = K·N, Var_DN = K²·Var_N = K²·N = K·S_DN, so slope = K (DN/e-). The (1/K) form only holds if K is defined in e-/DN, which contradicts '1電子あたりの出力K'.
image-sensor-048.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

interconnect-046.summary: EN choices 0 and 1 say 'which lowers resistance' where JA says 耐性が下がる (electromigration robustness decreases). In a wiring context 'lowers resistance' reads as lower electrical resistance, which reverses the intended (negative) meaning; choice 2 'improves resistance' is similarly ambiguous.
interconnect-046.basis: JA: 多孔質構造で、耐性が下がる / アモルファス構造で、耐性が下がる / ...耐性が高まる — refers to electromigration resistance (the question asks how it affects electromigration).
interconnect-046.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

ion-implant-018.summary: Says resist must be "several times" the ion range (Rp + several ΔRp). The usual masking criterion is thickness >= Rp + m·ΔRp evaluated in the resist (m about 3-5); requiring several times that is not necessary and misstates the rule.
ion-implant-018.basis: Standard mask-thickness criterion (e.g., Plummer/Deal/Griffin, Silicon VLSI Technology): choose d so that the transmitted fraction (tail beyond d of the Gaussian in the mask material) is negligible, i.e., d = Rp + m·ΔRp with Rp, ΔRp for the mask material. The lower density of resist is already accounted for by using resist Rp (larger than in Si), not by a multiplier.
ion-implant-018.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

ion-implant-047.summary: Note for choice 2 ("電気抵抗と磁気抵抗") reads "抵抗の種類ではありません" / EN "These are not kinds of resistance", which literally says electrical resistance and magnetoresistance are not kinds of resistance (false). Intended meaning is that ion energy loss is not described by them.
ion-implant-047.basis: Electrical resistance and magnetoresistance are, by definition, kinds of resistance; the note should reject them as energy-loss mechanisms.
ion-implant-047.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

linker-loader-005.summary: For a C program, the explanation says a difference in arguments can turn the call into a different symbol name. C does not mangle names, so an argument/signature mismatch does not change the symbol (it links, with undefined behavior); only C++ name mangling does that. EN repeats it ('signature mismatch').
linker-loader-005.basis: C compilers emit the plain identifier (e.g. foo or _foo) regardless of parameter types; argument types are encoded only by C++ name mangling (cf. linker-loader-035 in the same category).
linker-loader-005.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

lithography-001.summary: R from the Rayleigh formula with k1=0.27 is a half-pitch (≈39 nm), but the text says 'pitches finer than this need multiple patterning or EUV', which implies a ~39 nm pitch limit. The single-exposure pitch limit is ~77–80 nm, as lithography-005 itself states ('ピッチ約80 nm').
lithography-001.basis: 0.27×193/1.35 = 38.6 nm = half-pitch; pitch = 2R ≈ 77 nm. k1=0.25 is the half-pitch limit (lithography-021), so R is a half-pitch. lithography-005 gives the ArF immersion pitch limit as about 80 nm, so 001 contradicts 005 by a factor of 2.
lithography-001.by: AI audit (reviewed by maintainer), not human expert review

lithography-012.summary: Stage acceleration stated as 'a few m/s²' (数m/s²). Modern scanner stages accelerate an order of magnitude faster: tens of m/s² (several g) for the wafer stage, and more for the reticle stage.
lithography-012.basis: ASML's High-NA (EXE:5000) material gives wafer stage 8 g (~80 m/s²), twice the NXE wafer stage (~4 g ≈ 40 m/s²), and reticle stage 32 g. Even older scanner patents cite reticle accelerations of 0.5–4 G. So 'a few m/s²' (<1 g) is about 10x too low for current tools. Source: asml.com '5 things you should know about High NA EUV lithography' (2024).

logic-038.summary: States that a JK flip-flop with J and K tied to 1 'is' a T flip-flop. lithography-018.summary: The standing-wave parenthetical '縦方向の縞' is ambiguous in Japanese, and every translation renders it as 'vertical stripes' (en 'vertical ripples', de 'vertikale Streifen', fr 'stries verticales', nl 'verticale strepen', ko '세로 줄무늬', zh '縱向條紋'). That gets the orientation wrong.
lithography-018.basis: Incident light and light reflected from the substrate form a standing wave along the film normal, with intensity maxima and minima every λ/(2n) (about 57 nm for ArF in a resist with n≈1.7). The exposure therefore varies with depth, giving bright and dark layers parallel to the wafer. On the developed sidewalls these appear as horizontal ridges ('scalloping'), not as vertical stripes. The ja '縦方向の縞' is only correct if read as 'striped along the vertical direction', and the translations took it the other way. The fix rewords the parenthetical so it says the bright/dark pattern repeats through the depth, in all languages.

etching-035.summary: The explanation attributes the negative DC self-bias of a capacitively coupled electrode solely to electrons being more mobile than ions, and states it as holding for any such electrode. The condition that actually produces a nonzero DC self-bias, namely the powered (wafer) electrode being smaller in area than the grounded electrode/walls, is missing; without it the statement is false.
etching-035.basis: Electron/ion mobility difference makes every RF sheath rectifying, so each surface sits negative relative to the plasma on time average. The DC voltage that builds up across the blocking capacitor (the self-bias measured from ground) comes from the asymmetry of the two sheaths: by the Koenig-Maissel area relation V1/V2 = (A2/A1)^q (q ~ 1-4), the smaller electrode gets the larger sheath voltage. For a symmetric discharge (equal electrode areas) the DC self-bias is zero even though electrons are still far more mobile (Lieberman & Lichtenberg, Principles of Plasma Discharges and Materials Processing, ch. 11, capacitive discharges / asymmetric discharges). Real etchers have a small wafer electrode and large grounded chamber walls, so the keyed answer stays correct; only the mechanism sentence needs the missing condition.
etching-035.by: AI の点検(2回目の全問点検。指摘の根拠を保守担当が確認)
